sections.title: Anatomy: The Angle Landmarks (Schwalbe to Ciliary Body)
content: 1. Schwalbe's Line: Termination of Descemet's membrane.
2. Non-pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Posterior to Schwalbe's.
3. Pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Primary site of aqueous outflow.
4. Scleral Spur: The most anterior projection of the sclera; attachment site of the ciliary muscle.
5. Ciliary Body Band: The vascularized, darker, most posterior structure visible.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Blood in Schlemm's Canal (high episcleral venous pressure)
Exfoliation material on the trabecular meshwork

content.mnemonic: I Can See The Scleral Spur
content.explanation: I (Iris) - C (Ciliary Body) - S (Scleral Spur) - T (Trabecular Meshwork) - S (Schwalbe's Line). Posterior to Anterior.

sections.title: Technique: Dynamic Gonioscopy
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic; ensure patient is upright or supine.
Step 2: Apply gonioscopy lens (e.g., Goldmann 3-mirror or Posner 4-mirror) with viscoelastic coupling agent.
Step 3: Keep the beam narrow and vertical (1-2mm width) to avoid light-induced pupil constriction.
Step 4: Use indentation (compression) gonioscopy to differentiate appositional from synechial closure.
Step 5: If angle opens under compression, the closure is appositional (potential for LPI).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Imaging vs. Gonioscopy
content: AS-OCT (Anterior Segment OCT): Non-contact, high resolution (5-10 microns). Useful for objectively measuring AOD500 (Angle Opening Distance at 500 microns).
UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): 35-50 MHz frequency. The gold standard for visualizing structures behind the iris (e.g., ciliary cysts, ciliary body position).
Note: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard as it allows for direct observation of pigment and PAS that OCT may miss.
